1442905,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.10.1.2,1946-08-26,b8094e9f-95f3-46b2-ab3e-9e132f32ed9e,ca.m.8036,Mr. ANGUS MacINNIS (Vancouver East):,,LABOUR CONDITIONS,STEEL STRIKE-FURTHER DEVELOPMENTS-REQUEST THAT DEPUTY MINISTER ACT AS COMMISSIONER,,I asked the Minister of Labour on Saturday if the controller had made any effort to get-in touch with the parties to the steel dispute, and I should like to repeat that question now. ,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Angus MacInnis,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b8094e9f-95f3-46b2-ab3e-9e132f32ed9e&Language=E&Section=ALL
1442906,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.10.1.3,1946-08-26,48fe0415-1454-43d8-a242-1562dedacc97,ca.m.2450,Hon. HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister of Labour):,Minister of Labour,LABOUR CONDITIONS,STEEL STRIKE-FURTHER DEVELOPMENTS-REQUEST THAT DEPUTY MINISTER ACT AS COMMISSIONER,,On Saturday I gave an open invitation to both sides, combined with the 63260-337

amendment to the order, at least to get in touch with my department or myself in an effort to bring about some degree of conciliation in this dispute. I have read some of the speeches that have been made over the weekend and I am frank to admit, Mr. Speaker, I did not get much encouragement from them. I am prepared to lend every effort in settling this dispute if there is any degree of sympathetic consideration by either side.

As to my hon. friend's other point about the deputy minister of labour, we have had two or three commissioners in this dispute already. I think it can fairly be said that I run a reasonably large organization which faces difficulties and complications, and the steel dispute is not the only dispute that is in progress at the moment. I want to tell my hon. friend frankly that I cannot have my senior officials running all over Canada trying to settle industrial disputes, because I have an organization stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific that has been set up to deal with just such matters. If my hon. friend has any contact with either side to the dispute I should be very glad if he would call them up and tell them, ""For goodness' sake quit making silly speeches,"" such as I read in the press over the week-end. This dispute, like the rain, must come to an end some time. It always stops raining. But you cannot settle any dispute unless there is a willingness to sit down and settle it.

,Liberal,,Humphrey Mitchell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=48fe0415-1454-43d8-a242-1562dedacc97&Language=E&Section=ALL
1442907,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.10.1.4,1946-08-26,b8094e9f-95f3-46b2-ab3e-9e132f32ed9e,ca.m.8036,Mr. MacINNIS:,,LABOUR CONDITIONS,STEEL STRIKE-FURTHER DEVELOPMENTS-REQUEST THAT DEPUTY MINISTER ACT AS COMMISSIONER,,I thank the minister. I appreciate that I was asking a great deal of him to ask that his deputy go in there. But I was paying a compliment to his deputy in making that request because I believe he would be acceptable, perhaps more acceptable than anyone else, to the employees there.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Angus MacInnis,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b8094e9f-95f3-46b2-ab3e-9e132f32ed9e&Language=E&Section=ALL
1442908,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.10.1.5,1946-08-26,48fe0415-1454-43d8-a242-1562dedacc97,ca.m.2450,Mr. MITCHELL:,Minister of Labour,LABOUR CONDITIONS,STEEL STRIKE-FURTHER DEVELOPMENTS-REQUEST THAT DEPUTY MINISTER ACT AS COMMISSIONER,,Much as I should like to do it, I must say that sometimes I wonder how physically I have stood up for the last five years, and I say that without trying to be facetious at all. I say it seriously, and I say the same thing of my senior officials too. I have not had a holiday since the war broke out; my deputy has not had a holiday since he has been with me, and that goes for many of the senior officials in my department. To ask us to run all over the country after grownup men who cannot conduct themselves like grown-up men is asking too much. After all is said and done, the trains are still running, and the aeroplanes, and if these people were anxious to settle disputes instead of trying to make martyrs of themselves or names for themselves, a great deal more could be accomplished. I passed through a similar diffi-
Labour Conditions

1442944,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.17.1.1.1,1946-08-26,,,,stagedirection,,,,"Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Prime Minister) moved the second reading of bill No. 253, to amend the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945.

He said: On July 5 of this year the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in a statement to the house indicated that a committee of officers of the Department of Justice and other departments had under close and continuous scrutiny the orders in council which derive their authority from the War Measures Act and of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945. The purpose of this scrutiny is to reduce to a minimum the num-
Emergency Powers",,,,

1442945,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.17.1.1.2,1946-08-26,,,,stagedirection,,,,"ber of such orders in actual operation. Each of these orders has been carefully considered with the departments more directly concerned. Appropriate action has been recommended to secure the elimination of all orders which are no longer essential to ensure an orderly transition from war to peace.

In his statement the Prime Minister divided existing orders into several categories, and gave the number of each. These figures represent the situation which obtained at the time they were compiled, as the committee continued its analysis and action was taken on its recommendation. The volume of orders in council appearing in each classification naturally varies. On July 5 the Prime Minister referred to a total of 7,103 orders under emergency powers. Since that time the committee has reviewed twelve more orders in council, while a further seventy-two orders in council have been passed under the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act and tabled in the house, of which twenty-six merely revoke other orders in council, but those have not yet been reviewed and included in the tabulation. Accordingly the total number of orders in council passed pursuant to the emergency powers to August 15 was 7,187. There was one passed on Saturday which was tabled here. It is of course difficult to have these tabulations right up to the minute. Of this number 4,207 have been revoked, have expired or are spent. This means that 102 have ceased to have effect since July 5. Some twenty-six orders are in process of being revoked immediately. Some 616 are to be allowed to expire with the expiry of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1946. It is considered that one hundred orders can be reenacted under the authority of existing statutes not of an emergency character. To this end departmental officials are at present taking the necessary action.

The outstanding treasury board minutes under the emergency powers authorizing war duty supplements for government employees now number 1,531. These have been considered and placed in three categories: those granted for special duties which have now come to an end, and the war duties supplements will also come to an end. Then there are those in respect to which special duties for which the supplement was originally granted will continue indefinitely. In this case the civil service commission is being asked to examine each individual case and make appropriate recommendations as to what change in classification the civil servant concerned should receive.
Then there are supplements about which some doubt existed as to whether the special

duties involved can be definitely or finally classified as apt to continue indefinitely. Each one of these is receiving separate consideration. All these will be dealt with, and I may say at once with respect to this whole matter that some five or six weeks ago instructions were sent to each department to examine every one of the orders and to have ready for consideration not later than the end of this year bills for- legislation wherever the government might feel it would be proper to recommend legislation to parliament to take the place of the emergency power.

The remaining orders in council are those which the Prime Minister indicated as constituting the real body of the government's existing emergency power. They number 709. Of this number approximately 225 have been in substance placed before the house during the present session in the form of draft legislation relating to such subjects as war crimes, unemployment insurance, reinstatement in civil employment of discharged members of the forces, control of atomic energy, control of explosives, air and navy cadets, control of narcotics, compensation to veteran airmen, and then the large body of orders in council which were dealt with by the veterans affairs committee and which provided for the demobilization and rehabilitation of members of the armed forces. The remaining 484 orders in council are the measures which may continue to be classed as emergency powers at the close of this session. This total includes orders in council which merely amend other orders appearing in the group. The subject matter was outlined in general terms to the house by the Prime Minister in his statement of July 5. As he then indicated, while world conditions remain critical it is not possible to state for what periods of time each of the powers conferred by this group of orders in council may be required. In some cases statutory authority may have to be sought at the next session.

As I have indicated to the house, these orders in council are under constant review and will be dispensed with at the earliest opportunity compatible with the national welfare. I do not know whether the house would wish to have tabled the classifications that have been made. There are quite lengthy lists of the numbers of the orders, their date, and a sort of summary statement of what they deal with. First, there is the list of the twenty-six .of which the repeal is being arranged immediately or is in process of taking place. Then- there is a list of 225 which it is felt can be disposed of en bloc as having been provided for by legislation enacted by parliament at this session. Then there is a list of 100 which
Emergency Powers

the interdepartmental committee, presided, over by the Solicitor General, are recommending to be reenacted under other powers existing in general statute to the end sought. They are regulations which can be continued under powers that existed prior to the coming into operation of the War Measures Act, and the recomimendation. there is that they be taken out of that category and each placed under the general statute to which it properly appertains. Then there are 268 of another category. That appears to be a large number, but there are very many of them-which are just amendments of other orders and with respect to which there will have to be a recommendation by the government to parliament at the next session to enact legislation. They are the orders relating to the labour code; the wartime prices and trade board; rent control; the control exercised over cereals or other food products with respect to which the government of Canada has entered into contracts with other governments. They exist by virtue of the powers resulting either from the War Measures Act or from the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, but they will be required beyond the period when the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act will normally expire; and it is with respect to those that, the Prime Minister made the statement, which I understood at the time met with the pretty general approval of the house, that the government would ask to have the term of fifteen days after the opening of the next session extended to sixty days so that they could be dealt with by parliament at the opening of the next session instead of having to be dealt with at this session.

If I have the permission of the house I will table, without asking to have it included in Hansard, two copies of these lists, so that any hon. member who may wish to consult them will have an opportunity of doing so. Without going into the merits of emergency powers or anything of a controversial nature, I will submit without further argument that it would be in the interests of dispatch to have the amendment provided for by this bill, extending from fifteen to sixty days the duration of emergency powers after parliament meets at its next session, passed at this time so that it will not be necessary to have additional legislation to deal with these matters at this session.

There is this other consideration. At this time, if we were not to have this extension, we would have to provide for all possible contingencies and would have to ask parliament. to adopt more legislation than is apt to be required at the time parliament meets again I wish to remind hon. members that

the Prime Minister stated positively that it was the intention of the government at that time, and it still is, to have parliament meet towards the end of January, 1947, for the next session. We are conscious of the fact that hon. members made that quasi-undertaking a condition of the position they took when the Prime Minister announced in July that there would be this request to extend the duration of emergency powers until sixty days after the next session opens. I would therefore hope that at this time it will be the pleasure of the house to adopt this amendment and leave us under the existing impression that we have to do our best to get rid of this wartime legislation just as quickly as it is compatible with orderly reconversion to do so.",,,,

1442946,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.17.1.2,1946-08-26,a519c7ba-e092-4c85-95fb-2519b2cbfc06,ca.m.8326,Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,EMERGENCY POWERS,"CONTINUATION OF ACT UNTIL DECEMBER 31, 1946, OR SIXTIETH DAY AFTER OPENING OF 1947 SESSION",,"I rise on this occasion not to comment on the administration of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act., but rather to state our position with respect to the bill now before us. As hon. members know, a year ago when this measure was brought in here we objected to it very strongly. We are still as much opposed to it as we were then; and if this measure were a measure to extend the duration of this act we would oppose it as strongly now as we did then. As the minister has indicated, if the house should meet in the middle of March next year this measure under the existing statute would terminate at the end of March. Under the new bill it would terminate at the end of March if the house met in January. The measure gives the governor in council power to do by order in council what ordinarily would be done by this parliament. That is the reason we objected to it. There was some intimation when the question was raised in June or July of this year that if there was an undertaking that the house would meet in January rather than in March there would not be strong objection taken to the measure. The reason for that was this. If we meet in January and the act continues in force until sixty days after the house meets, the act will be no longer in force than if the house met in the middle of March with the act continued in force for fifteen days as now provided Under these circumstances we did not object and are not now objecting to the bill.

But when we reach committee stage I am going to offer an amendment, which I think the government can accept, because it does not alter the spirit of the amendment moved by the minister. I see no reason why a measure of this kind should be tied to a movable date. Why should we say that this
Emergency Powers
measure remain in existence for fifteen days after the house meets when we do not know when the house will meet? The amendment I shall propose at that time will be this:
To add after the word ""forty-seven"" in line 14 the following words:
or on the thirty-first day of March, one thousand nine hundred and forty-seven, whichever date is the earlier.""
The clause would then read as follows:

(1) Subject as hereinafter provided, this act shall expire on the thirty-first day of December, one thousand nine hundred and forty-six, if parliament meets during November or December, one thousand nine hundred and forty-six, but if parliament does not so meet it shall expire on the sixtieth day after parliament first meets during the year one thousand nine hundred and forty-seven, or on the thirty-first day of March, one thousand nine hundred and forty-seven, whichever date is the earlier.

I have done a little studying of this matter in ""The Law and Custom of the Constitution"", by A. V. Dicey. The thing which interests me is the opposition there has been to orders in council down through the years of British parliamentary history; and when you get to the end, this at least is clear, that there are recognized only two methods of legislation: one, which is frowned upon, orders in council; the other, acts of parliament. 1442970,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.18.1.2,1946-08-26,2b02ca65-52af-436d-9739-c9565c0af670,ca.m.2430,Mr. HUGUES LAPOINTE (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence) :,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence,MILITIA PENSION ACT,"AMENDMENT RESPECTION PENSIONS, ALLOWANCES AND GRATUITIES",,"As the minister pointed out on Friday last when he introduced the resolution to the house, briefly this act tries to bring into conformity with the Civil Service Superannuation Act the present Militia Pension Act. In view of the fact that the provisions of the Militia Pension Act, and also those of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act, appertaining to service pensions of members and benefits for their dependents, were not uniform with the provisions of other long-service pension plans of the federal government, there was established by treasury board minute a committee to review these acts, having in mind the provisions of the Civil Service Superannuation Act, and to recommend legislation aiming at the attainment of a degree of uniformity with the latter statute. The treasury board minute stated that the committee was to make its examination on the understanding that the changes which might be made would not apply to any member of the forces now under the respective acts unless such member so elected. The house might be interested to know that this committee was presided over by Mr. G. D. Finlayson, superintendent of insurance and comprised representatives from the three services, the financial superintendent of the Department of National Defence, and the director of the superannuation division of the Department of Finance, together with members of the staff of the treasury board to help them in their work.

The present bill is the one which was drafted by this committee, and it has the recommendation of the committee. The bill, as the explanatory notes indicate, is twofold in its scope. Sections 1 to 5 are for the purpose of amending and bringing up to date the existing provisions of the Militia Pensions Act so as to permit time served on active service during the last war to be included in the pensionable term of service of persons appointed to the permanent forces prior to April 1, 1946 and also to provide for minor amendments in part II of the act, which relates to the naval service, consequent upon certain administrative changes therein. The remaining section of the act adds a new part, part V, which is to be applicable to all persons joining the permanent force after March 31, 1946, in other words, all new
members coming into the post-war army and also those persons to whom the present act applies and who may elect to come under the new part.

The new part V provides that all persons to whom it applies shall contribute a percentage of their pay and allowances towards making good the pensions, gratuities and allowances specified in the part. It also makes provisions, to the extent therein provided, for the payment of allowances and gratuities to the dependents of all persons to whom this part applies. In these respects, this new part added to the act differs from existing provisions in that under the latter only officers and warrant officers were required to contribute to the pension fund, whereas on the other hand only the widows and children of those officers and warrant officers were eligible for any allowances and pensions. Part V conforms in principle and in substance to the Civil Service Superannuation Act, with such modifications and adaptations as were necessary to adapt the principles of that act to the particular circumstances of the armed services.

PROBE (Regina City):,,MILITIA PENSION ACT,AMENDMENT RESPECTION PENSIONS, ALLOWANCES AND GRATUITIES",,"I feel, as does the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Stirling) that this whole subject of permanent force pensions might well be referred to the study of a special committee. However. I wish to make a few observations on the bill which is now before us. The position at the present time is that when men have served for a period of years in the permanent military establishments of the country, and while they are still comparatively young, they are put on a lifetime pension paid by the people of Canada for the good service which they rendered while members of the permanent force.
Militia Pension Act

With the general thesis that a pension should be paid by the state to its servants there can be no disagreement. But when we consider the comparative inequity as 'between the permanent force, in regard to service pensions, and civilians in other walks of life, both members of the civil service and the people who have to buy annuities and pay for them, which annuities become pensions on their retirement from active work, then I think it is time some of us uttered a very strong protest.

I direct the attention of the house to the comments made by the auditor general with respect to the Militia Pension Act on page 47 of the .1945 accounts. Certain statistics which he gives are of interest and, I think, might well be put on the record:

In 1,938-39 there were approximately 1,400 contributors under the act. The number is now in excess of 4,800. The increases are mainly in army (from 1,000 to over 2,300) and in air (from 305 to 2,066). Contributions in 1938-39 were $179,027.16 and in 1944-45 the sum was $715,594.37.
That is the contribution by the individual in the service toward the pension fund.
On the other hand, disbursements by reason of awards increased from $1,548,537.55 to $2,227,534.95 in the same period.

That simply means that the government of Canada has increased the payment to pensioners by roughly fifty per cent in the period from 1939 to 1944. Putting it in still another way, in 1938-39 the awards under the pension act were roughly ten times the contributions made by the individuals who expected to benefit from the pension funds.

In 1944-45 the amount paid out in pensions was roughly three times the amount put in by the prospective claimants to pension. In other words the expenditure by the government itself, without any quid pro quo by the service persons was at the rate of $1,500,000 a year in 1944-45. To my mind there is no objection to the fact that the federal government is contributing to this pension. Do not overlook that. I shall come to that point in a moment. May I again quote from the auditor general's report:

It will thus be observed that current contributions represent about one-third of the outgo. In the 1944-45 fiscal year, 275 awards were made under the Militia Pension Act. In the case of those who were contributors prior to May 1, 1929, pension awards are computed on pay and allowances as of the date of retirement; in all other cases a three year average is applicable. A survey of awards made in 1944-45 shows that, when promotions have been frequent, the pension award generally approximates or exceeds the pay and allowances of 1939.

A table is given to illustrate the size of the pension in certain specific cases. I shall refer to a number of these examples to give the members of the house and the country generally an indication of what our permanent force people get by way of gratuity for the remainder of their lives from a generous government. Here is an example of a person who retired from the services at the age of forty-three,-a younger man than I am, and considerably younger than most hon. members in the house. He had had twenty-one years of service. In August 1939 he was a sergeant. He retired as a squadron leader. The pay and allowances which were considered for the purpose of computing pension under the act were at the rate of $4,210.51 a year. This gentleman, who is now forty-three years of age, receives a pension for life of $1,760.35. That, of course, is a fairly generous pension for a man who still has, I hope, many years of life ahead of him.

Let me give another example. It is that of an officer in the army who is now forty-seven years of age and who had twenty-eight years of service. Before the war he was a major. He retired as a major-general. At the time of his retirement he was receiving pay and allowances of $8,533.94 a year. By way of pension award we are giving him $4,947 a year. If he lives the normal life span I have no doubt that the country will be saddled with this very generous pension for anywhere from twenty to thirty or forty years. That is not the most extreme pension case.

It is quite true that under the proposed legislation, the new part of the act, this officer would probably be pensioned off. At present the statute does not permit of a pension in his case. All I can say is that when he joined the service he knew the conditions as regards both pay and pension, and he joined at a time when the regulations were such that no one could be pensioned before twenty years. Under special circumstances which are indicated in the act and of which he was aware, the officer is entitled to a gratuity of one month's pay per year of service, which would be eleven years, because I do not believe that the four years of Royal Military College service is pensionable service; but he cannot qualify for a pension under the act which legislated in these matters when he enlisted in the service. I shall be glad to have the case looked into, although my hon. friend says that has already been done. I do not know whether I shall be able to help, but if
he will give me the particulars I will see if there is anything that can be done toward helping this particular case. I am afraid that is all I can say.

The point I wish to make is that had he retired on his volition this summer it might be different; but he did everything he could to postpone his retirement, because he knew that the act would be amended. It would have meant only another month had he been allowed to remain in the active force for eleven years, and then he would have received the benefits of this act for the rest of his life. As it is now he will receive no benefit, other than a gratuity, which will not help him very much. There may be many others like him. A few years from now this man because of his physical condition, will be unable to do anything for himself. He will have no pension, and will have no way of making a living or supporting his family. I should like to appeal to hon. members of the committee in order that something should be done. I am not saying that this is exactly within the scope of the bill-I do not think it is-but there should be some way of dealing with cases of this kind.

1443050,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.18.1.81,1946-08-26,0bb58bfe-4a12-4783-bcd5-741d47c38b5b,ca.m.6121,Mr. PROBE:,,MILITIA PENSION ACT,AMENDMENT RESPECTION PENSIONS, ALLOWANCES AND GRATUITIES",,"As I see it, the actuarial value of a military pension after thirty-five years of service is considerably greater than the pension payable to a civil servant after thirty-five years of service, because a military pensioner may retire at age fifty-five and the civil servant retires at age sixty-five. I believe I am correct in that. Combined with that is the fact that for the purpose of the Militia Pension Act ""service"" includes service in the civil service. Suppose a man has been in the civil service up to about the age of fifty-two. He then decides that he would like to retire at the age of fifty-five. He says: I will have thirty-five years' service and I shall get a pension ten years longer than otherwise. I presume the parliamentary assistant can explain to the satisfaction of the committee that there is a safeguard which prevents a man from transferring at age fifty or fifty-two from the Department of National Health and Welfare to the Department of National Defence, the permanent force, staying there for a year or two and then getting a full pension because his employment in the civil service is counted in full, as I understand it. That is why I want this cleared up. Can a man transfer from the civil service to the permanent force a year or two before the age of fifty-five, assuming that in the normal course of events he will have thirty-five years' service in the civil service or the permanent forces by virtue of these regulations? What is to safeguard the government from having to pay an extra ten years' pension to a man who can get into the permanent force at that late date?

'My hon. friend will appreciate that because of the upset of war, and the transitional period through which we are now passing, there is bound to be a great gap there. column1: 1443109,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.19.56,1946-08-26,deccabc4-17c4-44e2-aa8d-18fcb0c9ca75,ca.m.3652,Mr. ROSS (St. Paul's) :,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,"Can the minister give an estimate of the total cost of the meteorological service of Canada?

,Progressive Conservative,,Douglas Gooderham Ross,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=deccabc4-17c4-44e2-aa8d-18fcb0c9ca75&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443110,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.19.57,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,The present cost of the service is about $3,500,000 per year. What it will be, I do not know.

1443111,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.19.58,1946-08-26,deccabc4-17c4-44e2-aa8d-18fcb0c9ca75,ca.m.3652,Mr. ROSS (St. Paul's):,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Surely there is some plan in contemplation. People are a little critical about the amount of money being spent on these meteorological services as compared with the amount spent previously. .
Supply-Transport-Air Service

,Progressive Conservative,,Douglas Gooderham Ross,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=deccabc4-17c4-44e2-aa8d-18fcb0c9ca75&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443112,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.19.59,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,My hon. friend says he is a little critical, but I am more critical. Facilities were greatly enlarged during the war. Stations were built in the north and in Newfoundland, and the services throughout Canada were enlarged to take care of the military airdromes. The greater frequency of service on the airways made it necessary to enlarge the staffs there. Radio-sonde is a new and expensive development which involves the sending up of balloons equipped with radio in order to obtain details of weather conditions at the higher strata of the atmosphere. All in all we are giving a vastly better weather service than before the war, and a vastly more expensive service. I am endeavouring to find out to what extent the cost can be reduced. This estimate is about the war time level, but I hope to be able to present estimates in the future that will show a reduction.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443113,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.19.60,1946-08-26,82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a,ca.m.8707,Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario):,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Is there any way other than by going through all the estimates and picking out items here and there by which we can get the full cost of the meteorological service, so that we can form a judgment upon it? Is there available anywhere a full statement and breakdown of the cost?

,Progressive Conservative,,James MacKerras Macdonnell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443114,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.19.61,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,There is no single vote covering everything, but the cost can be found by adding three figures together-the normal aviation figure, the reconversion figure, and the figure in the supplementary estimates. Another reason for the cost being greatly in excess of pre-war is aviation across the ocean. The expenditure on transatlantic aviation is very heavy indeed. It is not stabilized as yet, but is is hoped that the cost of operating can be stabilized within the next year, so that a better picture of the cost can be shown than is the case to-day. Canada is responsible for the transatlantic service, as regards both Canada and Newfoundland, and the cost is a heavy item.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443115,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.19.62,1946-08-26,deccabc4-17c4-44e2-aa8d-18fcb0c9ca75,ca.m.3652,Mr. ROSS (St. Paul's):,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Is there an arrangement by which the United States and other countries share the cost of the meteorological service?

,Progressive Conservative,,Douglas Gooderham Ross,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=deccabc4-17c4-44e2-aa8d-18fcb0c9ca75&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443116,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.19.63,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Yes. In the war Canada

assumed responsibility for weather services across the north Atlantic to the extent of facilities in Canada and Newfoundland. PICAO is studying a fair allocation of the cost of all weather services between all users, and if Canada is paying more than her share we shall be compensated for any surplus, and if we are paying less than our share we shall be charged accordingly.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443117,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.19.64,1946-08-26,82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a,ca.m.8707,Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario):,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,I would ask the minister if he does not think it would be reasonable in future to have a statement compiled showing the full cost of the meteorological service so that we could judge it intelligently. I am not going to waste more time on that now.

,Progressive Conservative,,James MacKerras Macdonnell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443118,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.19.65,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Next year there will be only two sets of items, in the main estimates and in the supplementaries. This year there are three, because the treasury board believed that a year of transition was necessary for it to be able to measure the expenditure properly. That is, the direct peace time expenditures can be shown against earlier peace time expenditures, and the transition expenditures can be shown against the war expenditures. The supplementary items are over and above anything contemplated when the main estimates were prepared. This is the last year for transition estimates.

There are places where electricity is supplied for only a certain period of the day. In my district particularly, it is supplied from six o'clock in the evening on. Some people think they should be given the same consideration as owners of battery sets, and I agree with them. In my district the Canadian Pacific Railway Company with its usual generosity supplies electricity only from six o'clock at night to six o'clock in the morning. I believe the people in that district should have the same consideration as owners of

battery sets. I took the matter up with the department and it received official recognition by an official in the department. I was given to understand in writing that my suggestion would be put into effect. Later on, some other official had the idea that it should not be put into effect and he cancelled the previous order. It was embarrassing to a member of parliament. On receipt of the letter from the first official I sent out the information to my constituents telling them that it would be done. Then the other official cancelled it, and as that happened: in June a year ago it was most embarrassing to me. I suggest to the minister that it is a reasonable request, particularly in places where power is supplied, as in this particular instance, only from six o'clock at night to six o'clock in the morning. These people should have the same consideration as the owners of battery sets; it would mean a reduction of only fifty cents, as I understand it.

It is pretty hard to make other classes for places where the current is on for only certain hours of the day. I hardly think that would be possible.

,Progressive Conservative,,Agar Rodney Adamson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=3f27b0a5-3b86-4f3a-8bab-f44a940c0742&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443223,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.19.169,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,The policy is not; but the actual licensing is under this department. This department is responsible for the administration of radio telegraph communications. In other words, my hon. friend could not put in a frequency modulation broadcasting station unless he had a licence from the Department of Transport. The Department of Transport would issue the licence only on the recommendation of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which is in charge of policy in all broadcasting matters.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443224,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.19.170,1946-08-26,a6dd23dc-6a92-4fd2-838b-ec9126ccf2de,ca.m.8535,Mr. SMITH (Calgaiy West):,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,The minister has raised a most important point. Why is this under his department? I cannot figure it out at all as to why they are separate.

,Progressive Conservative,,Arthur Leroy Smith,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a6dd23dc-6a92-4fd2-838b-ec9126ccf2de&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443225,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.19.171,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,There are many more uses for radio channels in the air, in other branches of communication, than there are in connection with radio broadcasting. Radio broadcasting is but a small band in the radio spectrum, whereas there are very large bands used for other purposes. It is necessary that all bands of the spectrum be controlled by one department. That is to prevent encroachment from one band to another. For example, there is far more radio used in connection with radio beams than in connection with broadcasting. For that reason, and on account of the international aspects of the policing of the radio airways, it is under one act called the Radio Act. That act is administered by the Department of Transport which is, by far, the largest user of the airways.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL

I should also like a statement from the minister with respect to the present situation as regards Caandian requirements for 1946-47; and also as to the subsidies being paid for the production of coal in Canada at the present time, particularly eastern Canada. 1443306,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.2.8,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,Mr. Justice McLaurin, a member of the royal commission, assured me that the writing of the report is well under way and that it will be in the hands of the government within the next two months.

The coal situation as far as eastern Canada is concerned is far from good. Bituminous coal is coming in from the United States fairly well at the moment, but we have had serious interruptions. Between the coal strike in the United States and the shipping strike on the great lakes we lost some six or seven weeks of shipments; and while the shipments are coming in now at better than normal rates, the deficiency in bituminous coal has by no means been made up. However, we hope that by continuing shipments up to the close of navigation we shall have enough coal in eastern Canada to carry industry through the winter. The situation in connection with industrial coal is much better than the situation in connection with domestic coal. In
Supply-Demobilization

domestic coal we hope to have about sixty-five per cent of our total requirements by the end of November, and prospects are that after that we shall have to depend on hand-to-mouth shipments and on coke which we can take away from our steel operations. The situation is by no means clear. We have undertaken a movement of coal from Alberta, which is helping out to some extent, but there is a serious deficiency in imported coke. Some is available this year, whereas last year we imported about 1,300,000 tons from the United States. This year we are importing less than half that amount from the United States for the reason that we are unable to buy coke in greater quantities from that country. Supplies of anthracite compare fairly well with the supplies last year. It is the serious decline from 1,300,000 tons of coke which is causing us worry. Just how we shall overcome it I am not sure. However, we shall keep fighting as long as the requirement exists.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443307,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.2.9,1946-08-26,316a4590-070e-4777-a3e9-b6985e3a9df3,ca.m.9932,Mr. BLACK (Cumberland):,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,Would the minister make a statement as regards the present rate of shipment of coal from Nova Scotia to central Canada? Those of us who were concerned with the securing of this market in central Canada for our surplus production, some fifteen or eighteen years ago, in Nova Scotia are very much concerned and disappointed regarding the volume of coal available for use in. central Canada. At that time we aimed at a million, a million and a half or two million tons annually exported from Nova Scotia to central Canada. During the war years we realized that the local demands had increased greatly in the maritime provinces, and for bunker coal as well, and we could understand why there was a curtailment of shipments to central Canada. We secured this market after great effort and with the sympathetic consideration of the people in central Canada, and we hoped to hold this market, once gained, for future years. I for one was hopeful that the people of Nova Scotia would respond to the requirement in central Canada and make special efforts to supply it, I may say that in our efforts over the years the master mind in this part of Canada was Mr. Frank Neate, who had a thorough understanding of the markets, the quality of the coal, our capacity to produce the cost of trans-portating, and, I might say, the obligation upon the people in Nova Scotia to supply these markets. Some weeks ago the minister gave me a statement that he was fearful that thf total supply from Nova Scotia for shipment to central Canada in the current year would not exceed 350,000 tons. Really it was put at $10 million in the expectation that an agreement would be entered into with the provinces which would call for joint expenditure on certain types of public works. The purpose of those visits was to see what urgent work was required and to make sure that the work was fully planned at this time so that it could be used as a balance-wheel to any sudden drop in employment. The proposal which the dominion government made to the provinces was that if the work was filed as a fully planned project it would be entitled to a twenty per cent grant at the time, if carried out at the time the government said the work was needed.

1443429,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.14.1,1946-08-26,deccabc4-17c4-44e2-aa8d-18fcb0c9ca75,ca.m.3652,Mr. ROSS (St. Paul's):,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,"Would the minister give us a few words of explanation about this item?

,Progressive Conservative,,Douglas Gooderham Ross,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=deccabc4-17c4-44e2-aa8d-18fcb0c9ca75&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443430,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.14.2,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,This vote covers a number of more or less clean-up items. The first has to do with Canadian Arsenals. A nucleus of war production capacity was established, the purpose being to make it possible to produce any article that was produced during the war in the permanent arsenals set-up. Specialized equipment was taken over from a number of plants and moved into the establishments which are included in the arsenals set-up. The cost of operating Dominion Arsenals for the full year is included in this item and it amounts to $3,600,000. It is probable that that is an outside figure because the practice of Canadian Arsenals is to charge for work carried on. A nucleus personnel must be kept on and there must be funds with which to pay that nucleus, but if a fair amount of work is provided by the services for the arsenals it is probable that they will be self-sustaining. The $3,600,000 is estimated to be the cost of operating the arsenals on a minimum basis.

The Dominion Arsenal at Quebec is put in as a separate item. This is the cartridge case and small arms division, and the amount provided is $1,828,940, for expenses of operating Quebec arsenal. I might say that that is much less than the pre-war vote for the same arsenal. Then the operating expenses for Chalk River are included, this amount being $4,500,000 which it is estimated will be needed to operate this plant for a full year.

Then, in connection with the winding up of crown operations I might say that when the actual work stops expenses go on for a time. This item is included to cover the cost of liquidating these crown companies. It includes operating companies such as Canadian Arsenals, Eldorado Mining and Refining Com-
Supply-Demobilization

pany, Park Steamship Company, Polymer Corporation, War Assets Corporation and Wartime Housing Limited. In some cases the winding up of companies involves a loss arising out of operating expenses during the winding-up period, and in this connection there is a long list of some thirty companies, which I shall be glad to read if my hon. friend wishes this information. The amount here is $10,071,060 for winding-up costs of these crown companies, making a total of $20,000,000.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443431,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.14.3,1946-08-26,deccabc4-17c4-44e2-aa8d-18fcb0c9ca75,ca.m.3652,Mr. ROSS (St. Paul's):,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,I suppose the arsenals which are to be operated now will be more or less pilot plants so that we shall be able to make anything we want and carry on experiments?

,Progressive Conservative,,Douglas Gooderham Ross,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=deccabc4-17c4-44e2-aa8d-18fcb0c9ca75&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443432,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.14.4,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,The arsenals are publicly owned plants designed for the purpose of making small quantities of everything that the forces may require. The understanding is that larger quantities would be made by private industry based on shop practices established in Canadian Arsenals. The net result will be that Canada will be much better equipped to move into the large-scale production of war material than she was when the present war broke out.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443433,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.14.5,1946-08-26,deccabc4-17c4-44e2-aa8d-18fcb0c9ca75,ca.m.3652,Mr. ROSS (St. Paul's):,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,This is similar to what we suggested in this house many years ago, that we should have arsenals capable of keeping a number of men employed so that we would be able to move into large-scale production and have trained workmen who would be available as foremen to carry on the work.

,Progressive Conservative,,Douglas Gooderham Ross,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=deccabc4-17c4-44e2-aa8d-18fcb0c9ca75&Language=E&Section=ALL

1443437,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.1,1946-08-26,82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a,ca.m.8707,Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario):,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,"It seems to me that $25,000,000 is an astonishing large amount to be coming along as a supplement. Why is it that this vote could not have been calculated more accurately?

,Progressive Conservative,,James MacKerras Macdonnell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443438,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.2,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,It is entirely a revote. It was anticipated that a larger number of contracts would have been settled before the end of the last fiscal year. It is necessaiy to revote $25,000,000 in order to permit contracts to be settled this year which were provided for in the estimates of 1945-46, but which could not be settled until after that vote had lapsed.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443439,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.3,1946-08-26,82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a,ca.m.8707,Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario):,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,Why is it in the supplementary rather than the main estimates?

,Progressive Conservative,,James MacKerras Macdonnell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443440,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.4,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,Item 610 in the main estimates is for $50,000,000, but that item was made up before the end of the last fiscal year. It was expected that the outlay during the last fiscal year would have been greater than it was, and therefore, in addition to the $50,000,000 voted in the main estimates, it is necessary to make provision for $25,000,000 in connection with contracts which it was expected would have been settled in the last fiscal year and for which provision was made in the last fiscal year, but for which settlement could not be concluded.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443441,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.5,1946-08-26,122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4,ca.m.3194,Mr. FRASER:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,Would War Assets come under this item?

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Knapman Fraser,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443442,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.6,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,No. There is no vote here for War Assets, but I promised that War Assets could be discussed under an item in these estimates. If my hon. friend cares to discuss War Assets under this item I shall be glad to have him do so.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443443,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.7,1946-08-26,122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4,ca.m.3194,Mr. FRASER:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,I asked a question which was answered, but I have not the answer with me. The navy department gave a list of articles, such as Fairmiles, corvettes, et cetera, which had been turned over to War Assets and I should like to know what War Assets received. I am not referring to the inventory which the navy department handed over, because I know War Assets did not receive all that inventory. At Three Rivers two corvettes were turned over to War Assets, and we know for a fact that many things were taken off those boats. The same thing occurred at Hamilton. A number of people went through he boats, and dental and medical equipment and many other things were taken. I should like to know what was on the ships when War Assets took over.

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Knapman Fraser,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443444,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.8,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,If there was any pilferage, I suppose that material would not be included in deliveries to War Assets Corporation. We guard these boats as best we can, and if there has been theft it could not be avoided. The cost of guarding them was high, and that was one of the reasons why we wanted to make a quick sale while there was something left on them.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443445,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.9,1946-08-26,122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4,ca.m.3194,Mr. FRASER:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,You have now over 1,000 guards with War Assets?

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Knapman Fraser,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443446,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.10,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,Yes.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443447,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.11,1946-08-26,122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4,ca.m.3194,Mr. FRASER:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,How many employees altogether has War Assets at the present time?

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Knapman Fraser,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443448,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.12,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,About 7,000.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443449,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.13,1946-08-26,122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4,ca.m.3194,Mr. FRASER:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,Are you taking on more
employees at the present time?
Supply-Demobilization

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Knapman Fraser,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443450,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.14,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,No, we have passed our peak. As soon as we empty a warehouse we can. relieve ourselves of the cost of guarding it. The peak of the operations of War Assets was passed at the end of July. Up to then we had been receiving material faster than we had been selling it, but the peak has passed and we are now selling a little faster than we are receiving. That trend will accelerate during the rest of the year. So that the staff has passed its peak. My hon. friend mentioned 1,000 guards. Taking in the whole custodian branch of War Assets the number of personnel would be nearer 2,500.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443451,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.15,1946-08-26,122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4,ca.m.3194,Mr. FRASER:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,How many departments are there in War Assets?

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Knapman Fraser,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443452,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.16,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,A complete report of the

activities of War Assets was tabled a week or two ago. That would give the information. I dare say the figure of 1,000 guards who are acting only as guards may be about correct, but the entire staff having custody of the articles and materials that have been turned over to War Assets is nearer 2,500.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443453,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.17,1946-08-26,122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4,ca.m.3194,Mr. FRASER:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,What building material has War Assets at the present time?

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Knapman Fraser,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443454,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.18,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,It has no building material other than the material that comes from the demolition of buildings. It is demolishing buildings and salvaging the building material as rapidly as that operation can be carried out. Other than that it keeps no stock of building material.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443455,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.19,1946-08-26,122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4,ca.m.3194,Mr. FRASER:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,What about pipe?

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Knapman Fraser,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443456,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.20,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,No pipe, except as we take it out of the ground on some dismantled project.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443457,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.21,1946-08-26,122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4,ca.m.3194,Mr. FRASER:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,You had some new black iron standard pipe some months ago, I understand.

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Knapman Fraser,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443458,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.22,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,The inventory is turning over all the time; we may have it to-day and sell it to-morrow. Most of the pipe we get goes to Wartime Housing to relieve the shortage there, or to some other government project such as veterans housing. It is turned over promptly.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443459,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.23,1946-08-26,122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4,ca.m.3194,Mr. FRASER:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,What vehicles has War
Assets at the present time at New Sarum outside of St. Thomas?

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Knapman Fraser,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443460,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.24,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,We process vehicles as fast as they are turned over to us, allowing time for advertising and the preliminaries that have to be gone through in disposing of government property. I venture to say that War Assets never had in its custody any vehicle for more than two months.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443461,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.25,1946-08-26,122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4,ca.m.3194,Mr. FRASER:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,You did at that place.
Perhaps they were not under War Assets but under navy or army or air. But they were stored there for much longer , than two months.

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Knapman Fraser,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443462,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.26,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,We can deal with them only after they are turned over to us and after documentation is completed1. I still think I am right, and I am so assured by officers. We have never had a vehicle in the custody of War Assets for more than two months.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443463,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.27,1946-08-26,977c879d-f3fa-4fc6-bf75-daae2cabb25f,ca.m.6671,Mr. COYLE:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,That place is in my riding. I venture to say that there are 8,000 trucks sitting in the yard there to-day, and some of them have been there for over a year.

,Progressive Conservative,,Charles Delmar Coyle,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=977c879d-f3fa-4fc6-bf75-daae2cabb25f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443464,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.28,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,Who owns them?

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443465,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.29,1946-08-26,122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4,ca.m.3194,Mr. FRASER:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,The government owns them. You cannot pass the buck.

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Knapman Fraser,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443466,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.30,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,My responsibility begins on the day that official documentation is completed and the property turned over to War Assets. Before that, I do not know that they exist.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443467,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.31,1946-08-26,82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a,ca.m.8707,Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario):,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,Someone is at fault. Would the Minister of National Defence be the proper minister to ask about the matter? Surely we should not be put off with that as the final answer.

,Progressive Conservative,,James MacKerras Macdonnell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443468,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.32,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,The services can give you the date on which the trucks were turned over to War Assets, or I could if I had more time. The committee on war expenditures has been given that information. That committee was the place to get details of that kind.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443469,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.33,1946-08-26,122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4,ca.m.3194,Mr. FRASER:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,According to the answer I got, there should be just a few hundred trucks with War Assets at the present time, but I understand there are still thousands of trucks in that place. The information just does not jibe.

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Knapman Fraser,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=122985bb-8354-4928-95e2-c74d0fbd4fa4&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443470,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.34,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,The only trucks that War Assets has at this moment, so far as I know, are some trucks that were crated for shipment abroad. Some of them were being sold in Canada and some outside. Beyond that, we have no trucks in War Assets.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443471,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.35,1946-08-26,82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a,ca.m.8707,Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario):,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,The matter should not be left in that position. We have had the statement made on the responsibility of a member that thousands of trucks still stand there. The minister says that they have not been in the custody of War Assets. Surely, then, we have the right to ask the government as a whole for an explanation of this situation, which seems a preposterous one. We are entitled to know just what the position is with respect to these trucks. Surely this item can stand until we

have been given the information, which could be got to-day or to-morrow, or, if not then, the next day, and I presume we shall be here for a couple of days.

,Progressive Conservative,,James MacKerras Macdonnell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443472,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.36,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,This item has nothing to do with War Assets, but I said that War Assets could be discussed on this item.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443473,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.37,1946-08-26,82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a,ca.m.8707,Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario):,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,Then let the minister, who is more familiar with these matters, suggest another item on which it would be proper to raise this matter. But he did suggest that War Assets could be discussed on this item, and this question surely affects War Assets, or, if not, the Department of National Defence. Surely we do not want to have this thing just pushed out of sight on a technicality. We should have a statement from someone in the government who knows just what the situation is.

,Progressive Conservative,,James MacKerras Macdonnell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=82878bc6-6bd2-407b-b2cc-7745aec02c2a&Language=E&Section=ALL

In the matter of these vehicles which seem to be available, as far as the public is concerned, in such large numbers, I think the minister could very well give the committee a statement on the matter of declarations by departments of government to War Assets Corporation wherein materials which are declared surplus are left in the custody of the service concerned because War Assets Corporation said they did not have the man-power available to take over the materials. In circumstances like that there is, I think, the danger of manipulation.

I will try to illustrate what I mean. Various sendee groups, notably of the army and air force, attempted to turn over the contents of various buildings in various parts of this country to War Assets Corporation. The number of such declarations ran into several thousands at the time the committee inquired about them this spring. I have not here the minutes of the proceedings, but the exact number is on record of cases where War Assets Corporation stated that they were unable physically to inspect, check and take over the equipment which was declared surplus by the branch of the service. The result of that was something like this. People who are interested in what is contained in these buildings, if they have some means of finding out the contents, can go to War Assets Corporation, and if they are fortunate, secure a release from War Assets of that portion of the material in which they are interested. That actually happened in many cases, because the service organizations admitted to us in the war expenditures committee that some of the declarations they had made to War Assets Corporation had been taken over in part and that they were still custodians of various buildings with part of the equipment which they had' originally intended to turn over to War Assets.

That situation perhaps will-and you cannot persuade the man on the street otherwise- if it has not done so, lend itself to some form of favouritism or manipulation, because, if one consumer or dealer can go to War Assets Corporation and get some of the commodities which are contained in the building where these items are stored, and can secure the release of part of them, you still leave-the rest of them nominally within the control of the army or the air force, and the War Assets people can at any time say to a prospective buyer, if they

1443518,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.82,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,I will explain that. We had in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply a director general of industrial reconversion. The purpose of the director of reconversion was to get war plants converted into peacetime plants, and to maintain employment in bridging the transition.

The question came up as to the purpose to which a government plant would be put. We call for tenders on a building, and we may get a range in prices between $500,000 and $6,000. The director general of industrial reconversion then insisted that he should inspect those tenders to determine which buyer offered the most employment, If one was to be used as a dead building, and by that I
Supply-Demobilization

mean a dead storage building, and another was to be used as a manufacturing plant, that certainly gave a preference to the man who wished to buy it for manufacturing. In other words, he was buying it for a purpose which promised reasonably substantial and steady employment.

In that case a decision was made. Sometimes it was referred to me, but more often it was not. I do not suppose I have seen five per cent of the real estate transactions, but occasionally one would come to me for final decision.

But let me point out the discrepancy in my hon. friend's report. Let us suppose the man who wanted it for dead storage had bid $600,000, and the man who wanted it for a manufacturing plant had bid only $500,000. The man who wanted it for manufacturing was offered it at the higher tender, and unless he was prepared to pay the high tender he did not get the plant. Usually he was prepared so to pay; usually the difference was not as much as $100,000. But that was the determining factor in deciding whether a plant would go to a firm which was offering considerable employment, or the firm which was offering little employment, provided that the discrepancy in price was not too great.

The minister has spoken about the raising of bids of successful tenderers or successful bidders on pieces of real estate owned by War Assets Corporation. I know of one instance where that was done. I want to ask the minister if it is a fair statement to say that in the early days of War Assets Corporation that policy was not followed, and that the policy now followed with respect to sales of war assets was a complete change? That is my information and I should like to have some comment from the minister. While in recent times some of the criticism which applied in earlier days may have been removed-it is to be hoped that is so-is it not true that in the earlier days some of these allegations had foundation? 1443543,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.107,1946-08-26,795045ac-0a2d-489d-aac6-1477f9c815d1,ca.m.1278,Mr. GRAYDON:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,What part did the local reconstruction councils play in the sale of real estate when the factors of employment, warehousing, storage and so on were involved?

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Graydon,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=795045ac-0a2d-489d-aac6-1477f9c815d1&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443544,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.108,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,As I stated, the reconstruction councils acting through the director general of industrial reconversion passed on sales before they were made. I would not be absolutely sure that that was always true, but I know of no case where it was not.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Graydon,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=795045ac-0a2d-489d-aac6-1477f9c815d1&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443546,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.110,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,They were all abolished as at the end of August, The functions of the reconstruction councils had to do with government plans for full employment under the proposed dominion-provincial agreements. When the dominion-provincial agreements failed to materialize, it was felt that we were not justified in the expense involved in keeping the reconstruction councils alive.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443547,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.111,1946-08-26,795045ac-0a2d-489d-aac6-1477f9c815d1,ca.m.1278,Mr. GRAYDON:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,My understanding was that the expense involved was relatively small, and it seems to me that with War Assets still having substantial holdings of real estate to be sold there should be no change in government policy.

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Graydon,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=795045ac-0a2d-489d-aac6-1477f9c815d1&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443548,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.112,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,I know of very few indus-tiial plants which remain to be sold. The problem of reconversion is at least three-quarters completed. In other words, we now care very little for what purpose a plant is to be used, because the peacetime industries which were clamouring for accommodation a year ago have all been taken care of. I know of only one industrial property within thirty miles of Toronto that is for sale to-day and personally I do not care for what purpose it is used.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL

To my knowledge. there are some properties which have not jret been declared surplus.

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Graydon,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=795045ac-0a2d-489d-aac6-1477f9c815d1&Language=E&Section=ALL
