1443559,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.123,1946-08-26,eb20cb84-344e-40aa-b7af-f2a7ff88f1f5,ca.m.9512,Mr. CASTLEDEN:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,Among the returns in connection with the operations of War Assets is one dealing with machine tools and equipment. One of the favourite firms in Montreal which has obtained some of the larger equipment is the Associated Machinery Corporation, Balfour building, Montreal. This company purchased some $886,000 worth of machine tools and equipment. It is enlightening to see the way in which they have been handling these goods. I have an example of the type of thing that happens when an average man tries to deal with War Assets. We know that aeroplane producers in the United States are

doing pretty well, but when it comes to the small machine shop in a small town it is entirely different. This particular company was advertising honing machines, complete with 110-volt motor. This particular man thought it was good value and he decided to invest $75 for a machine. But when he got the machine he found it was in rather bad shape. The whole thing had been stripped and what he got was simply a frame which was absolutely useless. He wrote back and he was told that he had brought it on an ""as, is and where"" basis. However, he protested further and finally they gave him a credit of S15.

This is one of the recognized dealers of the department and this is the kind of thing whieh Canadian people have objected to tremendously. Of course the whole operations of War Assets are pretty much of a dilemma for the government, supporting as they do the present system of the distribution of surplus goods by War Assets, goods which the Canadian people have paid for already through taxation and goods whieh should be available to the Canadian people. The whole idea of War Assets, under our present system of economy is that these goods should be destroyed so as not to interfere with business. The minister says that ninety per cent of all the goods that are ever going to reach War Assets have already been delivered. How much has it cost the Canadian people for these goods, and what percentage are the Canadian people going to realize out of the operations of War Assets Corporation in selling these goods? Their whole policy seems to be: Do not let these goods get out into the hands of the people; whatever you do, see that the goods are destroyed rather than go into channels that will interfere with trade.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,George Hugh Castleden,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=eb20cb84-344e-40aa-b7af-f2a7ff88f1f5&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443560,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.124,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,My hon. friend differs somewhat from the policy followed by his own province. One of our dealers, and one that was most insistent on being made a dealer, is Crown Assets Corporation of the province of Saskatchewan. Distribution in that province is handled through that dealer organization because of that insistence. So why my hon. friend is so bitter about dealers I do not know. The only practical way of handling sales of machinery is through dealers for the very reason my hon. friend states. A machine is shipped out and the buyer is not satisfied. He thinks he has not received all the parts the machine should have. War Assets is doing a wholesale business, whereas a retail dealer can

1443562,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.126,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,I could give that by classifications. I could tell my hon. friend what proportion of the purchase price of real estate and buildings War Assets is receiving. I could give the percentage of recovery on machine tools. But take poison gas, for instance. It cost a great deal of money to produce and the recovery from it is nil. In fact, there was a very large bill against War Assets for disposing of it. 'Take fighter planes. The recovery on them is very small. A few types can be adapted at great expense to domestic uses but great numbers of them cannot be. The cheapest way to get rid of obsolete planes was the bonfire, but the bonfire was so disturbing to people that we adopted a new policy, which seems to work very well. We sold the carcasses of planes for $5 apiece, and if you drive through Saskatchewan or Alberta you will find an aeroplane carcass in almost every farmyard.

1443570,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.134,1946-08-26,3f27b0a5-3b86-4f3a-8bab-f44a940c0742,ca.m.9024,Mr. ADAMSON:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,Yes. Living in the country I find it very useful for hauling lumber, and, as I said, it amuses the children, who

love to drive it. It is amazing how young they can learn these things. I found out by mere chance that these universal carriers were for sale. In the United States press not a day goes by but what you see advertisements of war equipment for sale at the larger stores in New York. I mention one in particular. Macy's had an advertisement the other day of carburettors for the Merlin engine. The people bought them simply because they cost four or five hundred dollars originally and were selling at fifty dollars, and presumably a large amount of money went to the government and the agent in disposing of those carburettors. But there is very little advertising of these surplus goods that are for sale in Canada. The average man on the street has very little opportunity of seeing them advertised. The big stores do not advertise them. Take an article like flying boots, which are very useful and desirable in a country where there is lots of snow. I was in one of the larger stores in Toronto and they told me, ""Oh, yes, we get flying boots occasionally but they are all snapped up by the people who are in the store at the time."" I think a great deal more effort should be made by the agents to advertise War Assets goods that are for sale. Some people who are lucky and are in the store at the right moment are able to get them, but there are thousands and thousands of instances of goods which are considered unsaleable and are not advertised which could be sold. I believe that a great deal more effort should be made to advertise the goods which the department has for sale.

1443576,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.140,1946-08-26,0cd180b9-3a82-4810-b0ce-83bc28f5b7c5,ca.m.7237,Mr. ISNOR:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,Coming to the suggestion that this was a ""whitewash"" report, I deny that it was a ""whitewash."" Hon. members agreed, and so stated, that it was a very fair report. We were not going to condemn the government for something it had not done, merely to satisfy certain, hon. members who were not on the committee. We were not going to condemn War Assets Corporation for carrying on in a manner which they felt would bring the best returns to our country. Sitting there as chairman, listening to the evidence day in and day out during our deliberations, I say without fear of contradiction that War Assets Corporation has done an exceedingly fine job. It may have made mistakes. The armed services may have made mistakes; they may have destroyed in the early stages some useful material. But I should like to know of any other organization which could be set up that would handle a business of $226 million in the time in which they did it and perform a better job. It must be remembered that War Assets Corporation was brought into being without any previous experience of the kind; it had to establish a new structure; it had to bring into being an agency, first to collect, then to assemble, recondition and supply the market with these goods in such a way as, so far as possible, not to interfere with the regular sale of goods.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat referred to Macy's, New York, advertising war assets goods obtained from War Assets Association-""W.A.A."" The same thing applied here in Canada:
column2: Eaton's, Simpson's

column1: and other stores throughout the dominion advertised the very articles that he mentioned.
I remember they sold airmen's shoes retail for $12.50.

1443578,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.142,1946-08-26,0cd180b9-3a82-4810-b0ce-83bc28f5b7c5,ca.m.7237,Mr. ISNOR:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,But War Assets Corporation could not possibly retail those, as some hon. members-inexperienced members-may think. War Assets Corporation could not sell those through retail channels; it would not be profitable to do so; they would not get the net return which they are getting to-day. The corporation was set up for the purpose of disposing as rapidly as possible of surplus materials, and I think they are doing that in the
best possible way, in spite of what hon. members who were not on the committee, and have not had an opportunity of studying their policy, may say.

As regards the questions and answers, I do not know whether the replies received were satisfactory to all hon. members, but I believe that the officials of War Assets Corporation and of the armed services endeavoured, to the best of their ability, to give the information which was requested of them. I do not know of any case, with the possible exception of the question referring to repairs to ships, in which the information has not been given in a complete manner; and, as regards ships, I believe the request was made for the cost of repairs in connection with twenty-seven of them. Seventeen ships were covered in the first return and, if I recall rightly, seven in a later return, making twenty-four out of twenty-seven, and particulars as to the other three were promised as soon as the repairs are completed.

I could go on, Mr. Chairman, and talk at great length with regard to the evidence. There were over 1,200 pages of evidence. .It is almost impossible for the minister, with his great ability, to begin to give all the details; and even though the members of this committee endeavoured to follow the evidence as closely as possible, I question whether any one of them could being to answer all the questions which have been put to us this evening. I do not pretend to say that I could answer a good many questions; but, after carefully following the evidence, I am satisfied that the policy being pursued is bringing about the best results possible, taking a broad and wide view.

As regards the question which has caused so much discussion, hon. members have read about it in the newspapers; the magazines also have printed a lot of material, and we investigated the subject. We have not fully covered the ground, and we frankly stated so. We criticized the Royal Canadian Air Force for not keeping better records. We also referred to the sensational and extravagant statements made by one of the witnesses. I recall that one of the words used in the original report was struck out. We endeavoured to make it just as fair for one as for the other; in other words, we presented a very reasonable report.
I am sorry to have taken up so much time, but I thought that as chairman of the committee I should put on record these few words.

Moreover, I speak from the point of view of the average layman who reads the article and wishes to know whether it is right or wrong, and I cannot find the answer. What the hon. member for York West has said deserves more than passing consideration. He refers to the question of the selling of various war assets material. Those hon. members who come from rural districts know what a lot of money can be realized out of auction sales. I do not care what sort of material it may be; to others it may be so much junk but to the purchaser it may be valuable. I have never gone to an auction sale when somehow or another, whether because of the spirit that prevails on such occasions or whether it is something that gets into one's blood, everyone did not want to bid. I believe that far too much war assets material has been perhaps discarded as junk or has been destroyed, as the evidence seems to have shown from time to time, when much of it could have been realized and turned over to the dominion treasury. I do not know whether it is too late, but I regard that as a constructive suggestion. After all, a dollar is a dollar, and we cannot afford to pass up any chances in seeing to it that 'the last cent is obtained from these things. What the hon. member for York West has said with regard to retail merchandising might more emphatically be said with regard to auction sales. I am a great believer in auction sales from the point of view of the seller, the man who holds the sale, and for that reason I think the government might properly consider the suggestion of a humble adviser like myself so far as rural matters are concerned.

1443592,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.16.156,1946-08-26,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,I admit that high prices can be obtained at an auction sale, but the government is supposed to have a price ceiling. Suppose we had some automobiles in the field. We would get a tremendous number of bids and we might make money, but what about the man who paid above the ceiling price. He would prosecute War Assets. A tag must be put on, which is a ceiling price set by wartime prices and trade board, and then it becomes no action at all, because we receive far more bids than we can supply. It became, therefore, a question of drawing lots among the bidders to see who would get the article. That is inevitable if the government is to

obey its own price ceiling policy. It is common knowledge that an enterprising auctioneer bought up some old tractors in Ontario, took them to Manitoba and sold them at eight or ten times their value-I am toldi it was Yorkton, Saskatchewan. I believe the auctioneer actually bought one himself before he got through. A wonderful time was had by all. That is all very well, provided that no government agency is involved. My hon. friend will find, on reflection, that auction sales are not the source of revenue for the government which he may imagine.

column1: the government's responsibility."" The city was in no position to engage in a large-scale housing plan that might be temporary and result in unsightly slums when the houses were no longer required.

'It is a situation which became complex before it was recognized; but it should have been recognized before it became too complex to handle. And the government was in a better position to anticipate it than the city was.""

And so on. I discussed this matter at the beginning of the session. I pointed out that it was time the minister took responsibility in bringing the provincial and municipal authorities together so that it might appear as to whose responsibility it was. Here we are with a situation all across Canada much the same as was experienced here on parliament hill on Saturday. These men, veterans-of two wars, some of them with their wives, children and friends, paraded to parliament hill to appeal for assistance. One of the slogans read, ""Where are those homes fit for heroes to live in?"" And another, ""Have you ever tried to live in one room with a child?""
I suggest that the minister should make a statement as to what he proposes to do in this matter. He has now had more than a year since V-E day.
I have had a question on the order paper for weeks, and it is still there as question * No. 1:
What is the total value of construction permits which have been issued to breweries and distilleries in Canada since V-E day?

It is not that I am quarrelling with hon. members who wish to consume the products of these breweries and distilleries. But I think we should have some sense of priority, and some sense of values. I cannot see any good reason why permission should have been given for such large commitments for breweries and distilleries, at a time when housing continues to be Canada's No. 1 problem. 1443628,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.18.16,1946-08-26,20afcc72-88d0-433e-8b61-a7bcd98b2ec9,ca.m.3746,Mr. McILRAITH:,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,Yes, I know that. However, I took the precaution of counting them, and I believe some others did. However, I do not think anything turns on that, in any event.

There is no doubt that many of these veterans are in difficult circumstances so far as housing -is concerned. I happened to know personally a considerable number who were in the parade, and to know something about their personal circumstances. When they reached the front of the building they were received and, as a matter of fact, a subcommittee from among them, numbering about eight or ten persons, came to my office. The minister was kind enough to come in and receive them, along with the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, the hon. member for Ottawa East, and myself.

The statement about housing being a civic affair and that the city could have all the houses it wanted arose out of a question asked by a tenant in one of the present wartime housing houses on Carling avenue. This tenant recently arrived in Canada, for the first time; and when the question, was raised some discussion developed because the other members in the delegation did not have any housing, and had somewhat different ideas as to

what was needed. The question arose as to why we built only 200 last year on that particular project. An answer was given and an attempt made to explain that wartime housing houses are built in conjunction with and at the request of the municipality, and that the municipality has the responsibility of making the request. That is how the whole subject arose.

I saw the morning paper and I must say I was somewhat startled by the headline on the story. There was nothing wrong with the story; it had to mention only part of what went on, and not all of it; But the headline was a bit startling, to put it mildly. Those veterans had all sorts of difficult problems. One of them, who was a personal friend of mine, had come from the old country in 1934 to join the Canadian merchant marine. He served on the great lakes merchant ships in the summer, and on ocean-going vessels in the. winter. He never came to any town or settlement in Canada at any time prior to the war. Upon the outbreak of war he enlisted in the navy, and has a most excellent record of service. During the war he, was fortunate enough to marry an Ottawa girl. He has now applied for housing under a wartime housing project. Priority was given to persons who had residence in Ottawa at the outbreak of the war, so that he was shut out.
Mr. NICHOLSON; Where would his residence be?

1443633,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.18.21,1946-08-26,20afcc72-88d0-433e-8b61-a7bcd98b2ec9,ca.m.3746,Mr. McILRAITH:,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,,,That has been explained in the house several times. I think it is fair to say that the construction control was difficult to administer. There always was the cry, ""We in the local area know what is needed to reestablish our men. We know when someone wants to be reestablished in business. How can you, in the central government in Ottawa, know what should be done in other parts of Canada?"" Jurisdiction was given to the municipalities to decide, bearing in mind the needs of those particular municipalities. Many of them did not choose to exercise their power, although I believe some of them did. I understand that some municipalities do exercise the power and do reject applications for building permits for such things as have been under criticism to-night. Others do not.
But to say that there has been a passing of the buck on the municipalities does not quite meet the facts.

COLIN GIBSON (Minister of National Defence for Air):,Minister of National Defence for Air,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE,,The R.C.A.F. during the past six months has progressed rapidly with demobilization, with the result that to-day we have a strength which is less than our estimated post-war strength. That means that we have demobilized rapidly. We have not taken in recruits as rapidly as we should have liked, but we have set a high standard and recruits have been coming in satisfactorily up to the present time. Those who have been accepted for the permanent force number 9,122. Our total strength is 15,373, of which 1,515 are members of the women's division, who will be going out by the end of this year.

Our forces overseas have been repatriated rapidly, and at the present time we have less than 500 serving overseas. Some of them will be remaining there on courses and on duty, and the remainder will eventually come back to Canada.

To secure our list it would not have been fair to take them on a ""first come, first accepted"" basis, and we had to find out the approximate total of officers who were applying; we had to review their qualifications, and then decide what ranks we would be in, a position to offer them. Consequently, some officers whose records and qualifications were outstanding might be retained with the ranks they held at the end of the war; other officers might be required to revert to a lower rank; some officers we might not be able to keep in commissioned rank, and they were given an opportunity to enlist in one of the trades of the service. But that did take time, and consequently many who had applied for a permanent commission could not get a definite answer for several months. The list has been gone over thoroughly, and at present there are still some officers who are on the B list and who are being notified as to whether they have been accepted or not and what ranks they will hold.

With regard to the remarks made about our taking time to bring up our force to the required number, we could possibly recruit up to strength in a few months if we desired to lower our standard, but we have a high standard and we are endeavouring to maintain it at that level, because we believe that in the long run it will be beneficial to the air force to do so, instead of lowering the standard in order to get numbers rapidly.

1443761,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.21.71,1946-08-26,ea0e0f89-5c1d-4149-b665-08e87af67aa2,ca.m.5378,Mr. FERGUSON:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE,,I happen to know young men who had matriculated and who rose from the ranks during the war. Many of them cannot get into the air force now to satisfy their own desires. They did good service on bombing expeditions over Europe. They have applied to the government to go back as flying officers, and they have been told that their applications could not be accepted. I can hardly believe that some of these young men who have made their application to be taken into the air force are not of the standing necessary for the Canadian air force to-day. So far as they know, they were discharged A-l physically. They have a splendid active war record. No
Supply-Defence

explanation is given to them as to why they were turned down. They are simply told that their applications had been declined. I should certainly like to know the standard of qualifications necessary for an ex-officer of the Canadian air force in order that he may re-enlist in the air force which now requires approximately 2,000 additional men to fill the ranks. I think it is an awful slap in the face to young men who served their country during the war to tell them that they cannot come up to the standards which are required to re-enlist, when they are young men who were in a force of which Canada was so proud during the war. I know these men. They were not discharged physically unfit. I have seen their names mentioned in dispatches. I have seen the number of active flights, and active bombing expeditions that they took over Germany. They have matriculated. They have served in the ranks as officers and they have been mentioned in dispatches. They have made many flights over Germany. There are still 2,000 vacancies to fill, and these young men are the kind of men who are capable of filling them. What requirements must they have?

1443767,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.21.77,1946-08-26,ea0e0f89-5c1d-4149-b665-08e87af67aa2,ca.m.5378,Mr. FERGUSON:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE,,The young men I am referring to are now at the age of twenty-one or twenty-two, and apparently they had sufficient training to fly aircraft during the war. We still should be able to use their capabilities in training. I certainly agree with the hon. member for Vancouver North that the inducement of $100, on retirement, for each year served, is far from adequate to induce any young, red-blooded boy to join the flying force. He should have something to compensate him for his excellent service, and a necessary service to the country in these days. The condition in this country, and the condition throughout the world at the present time is one which should encourage young men of the right calibre to go into our flying corps. ,Progressive Conservative,,Julian Harcourt Ferguson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ea0e0f89-5c1d-4149-b665-08e87af67aa2&Language=E&Section=ALL
1443768,ca.proc.d.1946-08-26.20.21.78,1946-08-26,d7d1c6b0-bb86-473e-a28b-dcb4659d416e,ca.m.5243,Mr. MASSEY:,,DEPARTMENT OF RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY,DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE,,I was discussing the matter of recruiting and, although we got away from the subject for a while, we are back on it again. I certainly subscribe to what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver North in regard to the attraction that should be developed for the recruit. In the first place, the minister will realize that the type of lad he is after is the type of lad who is the cream of the crop; he must be. If he comes into the R.C.A.F. at the age of eighteen, nineteen or twenty, he will be leaving it on short-term commission when he is twenty-four, twenty-five or twenty-six. Those five years are pretty valuable years. We hope he will not be required for combat duty. If he is not, and he is retired, he has given in the service of his country, just as if it were at war, those valuable years. We can therefore afford to compensate him, and compensate him well. But he wants to know what that compensation will be.

I should like to say to the minister, with all the earnestness of which I am capable, that the more definite the information can be that will be given to the public at large, the more rapid his recruiting will be. One of the great difficulties up to the present time-and I am

quite sure the minister will understand what I mean by ""present""-has been that there have been a few feeble advertisements. I have seen them. They are small and, if the minister will forgive my saying so, they are not attractive. I say that as a former advertising man. They bring the name of the Royal Canadian Air Force to the attention of those who see it, but they are not particularly original, nor are they particularly good. Furthermore, they say very little.

In other words, the lad may be attracted by the advertising, and it may set him thinking. But it does not send him to a recruiting officer, saying, ""I want to enlist."" It sends him out to get further information. In other words, the minister relies upon the recruiting officer to sell the young man the idea. He is not sending the young man to the recruiting officer to enlist. In this way the burden is on the recruiting officer, because the lad has to go there first.

I believe there is a story to be told about the Royal Canadian Air Force in peace time, a story which is more attractive than perhaps many of the lads realize to-day, I believe the plans the minister placed before the committee this evening are good plans. But are they definite? Who knows them? If you are to recruit during a'war, that is one thing. If you are to recruit during peace time, that is another thing. The minister is in a position of-and I use the word in quotation marks- ""selling"" the Royal Canadian Air Force. He has the grandest air service in the world to sell, and it can be sold. But I feel definitely that a clear statement must be made in regard to what the lad's position will be when his training will start and, if he is going to enlist for aircrew, when his air training will start. He wants to know that. I realize the difficulty in the way of coming to that definite decision. But on the other hand, before we get either the quality that we want, let alone the quantity, that story will have to be told. So I urge upon the minister, with all the earnestness of which I am capable, that the story be told quickly. I am quite sure his 400 or 450 a month will increase rapidly.

While I am on my feet, I shall mention another matter. As the minister is probably aware, I can speak only for one release centre, namely No. 4 release centre. At that centre there were attached to the staff some eighteen officers as liaison officers, working in connection with employers. Those eighteen officers circulated through that portion of Ontario into which the releasees from No. 4 release centre went. The results of those contacts were good. If they did not already have it, employers were given a copy of the employers'
United, Nations

guide, which was an excellent publication. It was explained to them in some detail by the visiting officer. Further, the employer was chatted with in regard to his treatment of returned personnel. The net result was that the national employment service were definitely interested in the work we were doing, and finally there were attached to the national employment service two officers on the permanent detachment to work in conjunction with that office.

I know from first-hand information and first-hand contact that the results of having these two officers in the national employment service office in Toronto were most beneficial, since many of the ex-service men seeking employment felt much freer talking to someone in uniform who spoke their language than they did to a civilian who was simply there to see about their possible future jobs. Has the minister given any consideration to extending that particular service to other employment centres in Canada?

,Progressive Conservative,,Denton Massey,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d7d1c6b0-bb86-473e-a28b-dcb4659d416e&Language=E&Section=ALL
